claims.text: SiC is a crystalline wide-bandgap semiconductor suitable for phonon-dominated lattice heat transport.
The proposed SiC matrix is electronically insulating or has a negligible electronic contribution to thermal conductivity.
Nanoscale SRO precipitates can be embedded in a crystalline SiC matrix.
Embedding nanoscale SRO precipitates in SiC enhances phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering caused by SRO precipitates shortens phonon lifetimes or scattering times.
Shorter phonon lifetimes reduce the lattice thermal conductivity of precipitate-containing SiC relative to pristine SiC.
High-purity crystalline SiC can have minimal electronic contribution to thermal transport.
Compositional tuning and controlled thermal treatments can produce a controlled distribution of nanoscale SRO precipitates in SiC.
The introduced SRO precipitates can form a coherent precipitate phase within the SiC matrix.
At ambient to moderate temperatures, phonon-phonon interactions and nanostructural scattering dominate heat transfer in the proposed SiC system.
The density, size, and coherence of SRO precipitates mediate their effect on thermal transport.
SRO precipitates act as additional phonon-scattering centers.
Additional scattering by SRO precipitates limits the phonon mean free path.
A reduced phonon mean free path lowers lattice heat conductivity.
SiC containing SRO precipitates will exhibit measurably lower lattice thermal conductivity than precipitate-free SiC.
Heat conduction in pristine crystalline SiC is dominated by phonon transport with longer scattering times than in the proposed precipitate-containing material.
TEM or atom-probe tomography can characterize the precipitate size, density, and distribution in the proposed samples.
Inelastic neutron scattering or Raman spectroscopy can measure the relevant phonon lifetimes or scattering times.
The 3-omega method or time-domain thermoreflectance can determine lattice thermal conductivity in the proposed samples.
Failure to observe statistically significant reductions in both phonon scattering time and lattice thermal conductivity relative to the pristine control would falsify the hypothesis.
